newsitem.title: JORDAN: Jordan central bank reserves up a record $950 mlln.
newsitem.headline: Jordan central bank reserves up a record $950 mlln.

text.p: Jordan's central bank governor Ziyad Fariz said on Thursday foreign reserves rose a sharp 36 percent in the first half of 1997 to a record $950 million, buoyed by record foreign capital inflows.

Fariz said higher expatriate worker remittances, tourism receipts, export earnings and foreign investment inflows fuelled the rise in net foreign currency cash reserves from $697 million at the end of 1996.
"Foreign reserves have almost reached year-end (1997) target of $1.50 billion largely due to the improved performance of the economy and large inflows of foreign capital," Fariz said.

In the first four months of 1997, export earnings rose 8.2 percent compared to the same period last year, along with a 16 percent growth in remittances of Jordanian workers abroad and a six percent rise in tourism receipts.
Foreign investment, inflated global funds' recent unprecedented buying spree of blue-chip stock, injected a total $70 million in the same period, another central bank source said.
"This reflects a more positive investor perception of Jordan's investment scene," the source said.
Reserves are now close to an International Monetary Fund (IMF) three months import cover figure.

Fariz told Reuters he expected performance to improve further as a privatisation drive picks up later this year. A balance of payments surplus so far indicates the economy will hit a 6.5-percent growth rate in 1997.

Bankers also attributed the enhanced reserves to the central bank's more sophisticated monetary policy to better manage money supply, which has buoyed confidence in the local currency and encouraged more foreign currency transfers into dinars.

"Dollarisation in the economy is declining, and people are favouring assets denominated in the dinar because of the stability of the dinar and the high interest rates compared (to) the dollar," said Mifleh Aqel, regional manager, Arab Bank.

The central bank also plans to raise liquidity by setting an 8.0-percent target for money supply growth by year-end, which bankers expect will ease interest rates and inject more available credit for economic growth.
Central bank sources also said monetary policy would focus on boosting foreign reserves to protect the dinar's exchange rate, which has been fixed to the dollar since the end of 1995.
The source said it would preserve at least a three-percent interest rate differential between the local currency and dollar to encourage dinar-denominated assets.
"The dinar's attractiveness has increased," said the central bank source.
The bank official said inflationary pressures were under control with a below four-percent inflation on target for 1997.

The healthy foreign reserves situation has also made the central bank more confident to take measures to ease its high interest rate policy for the first time in more than 1-1/5 years to generate growth and activate local investment, bankers said.
Yields on Certificates of Deposits (CDs), a key benchmark for interest rates, fell on Thursday for the first time since early 1996 after introducing competitive auctions.
They fell to 8.825 percent from a previously fixed 9.25 percent while the six-month paper also dropped to 9.033 percent from 9.50 percent.
